sections.title: The People Pharaoh Tried to Crush
paragraphs: Genesis ended with Joseph and his family living in Egypt. Now the scene changes. Years pass, Joseph's generation dies, and the Israelites become a large, growing people. A new Pharaoh sees their numbers as a threat. Instead of treating them as neighbors, he makes them slaves. Under harsh taskmasters they build storage cities called Pithom and Raamses. The harder the Egyptians push them, the more the Israelites continue to grow.

Pharaoh then targets the most vulnerable. He orders the Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, to kill baby boys at birth. But the women fear the true God more than the king and refuse to carry out his cruel order. When questioned, they answer Pharaoh, and Jehovah blesses them for respecting life. Pharaoh escalates his command: every newborn Hebrew boy is to be thrown into the Nile.

That is the frightening world in which the next great Bible figure will be born. Pharaoh thinks he can control the future by hurting children. But the story is already showing something powerful: ordinary people, including two courageous midwives, can refuse to participate in cruelty.
sections.takeaway: Shiphrah and Puah are remembered by name, while the powerful Pharaoh isn't named in this account. Their courage mattered.

sections.title: A Baby in the Reeds, a Man in Exile
paragraphs: A Levite couple have a baby boy and hide him for three months. When hiding him is no longer possible, his mother makes a watertight papyrus basket and places it among the reeds beside the Nile. His sister watches from nearby. Pharaoh's own daughter finds the crying child and feels compassion. In a remarkable turn, the baby's sister arranges for his own mother to nurse him. Later Pharaoh's daughter adopts him and names him Moses.

As a grown man, Moses sees an Egyptian beating a Hebrew. He strikes the Egyptian, kills him, and hides the body. When news spreads, Pharaoh tries to kill Moses, so he runs away to Midian. There he helps women draw water for their father's flock, is welcomed into the family, and marries Zipporah. Their son Gershom is born while Moses is living as a foreigner.

Meanwhile, the suffering in Egypt hasn't stopped. The Israelites cry out under slavery, and Jehovah hears them. He remembers his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Moses is far away, living as a shepherd, but his story and the people's story are about to come together again.
sections.takeaway: The basket in the Nile didn't look like a rescue plan for a nation. Yet Moses' survival became part of a much bigger story.

sections.title: The Bush That Wouldn't Burn Up
paragraphs: One day, while caring for his father-in-law Jethro's sheep near Horeb, Moses notices a thornbush on fire. But something is strange: the flames aren't consuming it. He goes to look closer. Jehovah's angel appears in the flame, and Jehovah calls Moses by name. Moses is told to remove his sandals because he is standing on holy ground.

Jehovah says he has seen the suffering of his people in Egypt and heard their cries. He intends to bring them to a good land, a land flowing with milk and honey. And he is sending Moses to speak to Pharaoh. Moses asks a very human question: who is he to take on such a task? Jehovah assures him that he will be with him.

Moses also asks what to tell the Israelites if they ask about the God's name. Jehovah identifies himself by his personal name, Jehovah, and makes clear that he can become whatever is needed to fulfill his purpose. The God who made promises to their forefathers is now acting to keep them. This isn't just a rescue from bad circumstances; it is a chance for Israel to know Jehovah as the one who carries out his word.
sections.takeaway: Jehovah wasn't unaware of the people suffering in Egypt. He had seen, heard, and remembered.

sections.title: A Reluctant Messenger Gets Help
paragraphs: Moses is still worried. What if the people don't believe that Jehovah sent him? Jehovah provides convincing signs. Moses' shepherd's rod becomes a serpent and then a rod again. His hand becomes diseased and is restored. If necessary, water from the Nile can become blood. Each sign teaches that this mission rests on Jehovah's power, not Moses' cleverness.

Then Moses admits he doesn't feel capable of speaking well. Jehovah reminds him who gave humans the ability to speak and promises to help. Still hesitant, Moses asks for someone else. Jehovah appoints Moses' brother Aaron to speak on his behalf. Moses can deliver the message, and Aaron can help communicate it. Jehovah's arrangement makes room for the abilities of both men.

Moses prepares to return to Egypt with his wife Zipporah and their sons. On the journey there is a serious incident involving the circumcision of a son; Zipporah acts, and the danger passes. Aaron meets Moses in the wilderness. Together they tell the Israelite elders what Jehovah has said and perform the signs. For the first time in this story, the people hear that Jehovah has paid attention to their suffering. They bow down in worship.
sections.takeaway: Moses didn't suddenly become fearless. Jehovah gave him reasons to trust and a brother to help.

sections.title: When Deliverance Seems to Make Things Worse
paragraphs: Moses and Aaron stand before Pharaoh and ask him to let Israel go into the wilderness to worship Jehovah. Pharaoh's response is defiant: he doesn't acknowledge Jehovah's authority and won't release the people. That very day, he makes their work harder. Brickmakers must gather their own straw but still produce the same number of bricks. Israelite foremen are beaten when the impossible quotas aren't met.

The desperate foremen turn on Moses and Aaron. They feel the mission has made everything worse. Moses himself asks Jehovah why he has allowed more trouble and why the people haven't been rescued yet. The account doesn't pretend that doing the right thing always produces immediate relief. Sometimes the pressure rises before anything changes.

Jehovah responds by renewing his promise. He will bring Israel out of slavery, take them as his people, and give them the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But the Israelites are too discouraged by harsh labor to listen. Chapter 6 also gives the family record connecting Moses and Aaron to Levi; their parents are Amram and Jochebed. Even when the people can barely hope, Jehovah's commitment remains firm.
sections.takeaway: Discouragement wasn't proof that Jehovah's promise had failed. The rescue was still ahead.

sections.title: The Nile Turns to Blood
paragraphs: Moses is 80 and Aaron 83 when they confront Pharaoh. Jehovah gives Aaron the role of spokesman. Before Pharaoh, Aaron throws down his rod, and it becomes a big snake. The Egyptian magic-practicing priests imitate the sign, but Aaron's rod swallows theirs. Pharaoh still refuses to listen. The stage is set for a confrontation that will expose the limits of Egypt's power.

Jehovah instructs Moses to meet Pharaoh by the Nile. Aaron stretches out his rod, and the river turns to blood. The fish die, the Nile stinks, and its water cannot be drunk. Water in other places is affected too. The Egyptians dig around the Nile looking for water they can use. Their magic-practicing priests imitate the sign, but they cannot undo the disaster.

Pharaoh isn't persuaded. The first plague lasts seven days before the account moves on. Notice the contrast: Egypt's ruler can't guarantee clean drinking water, while Jehovah is showing that even the Nile, on which the kingdom depends, is under his authority.
sections.takeaway: A river that sustained a powerful civilization became the first sign that Pharaoh wasn't in control.

sections.title: Frogs, Gnats, and a Boundary in Goshen
paragraphs: Next come frogs—everywhere. They enter houses, bedrooms, ovens, and food containers. The Egyptian priests imitate the plague, but Pharaoh needs Moses to ask Jehovah to remove it. He promises to release Israel if the frogs go away. Once they die and the pressure lifts, however, he goes back on his word.

Then Aaron strikes the dust and gnats appear on people and animals. This time the magic-practicing priests cannot reproduce the sign. They acknowledge that God's power is behind it, but Pharaoh remains stubborn. The fourth plague brings swarms of gadflies that ruin conditions throughout Egypt. Jehovah makes a distinction: the Israelite region of Goshen is spared.

Pharaoh tries negotiating. First he says Israel can worship within Egypt; then he offers to let them travel into the wilderness. Moses insists that Jehovah's instruction must be followed. Pharaoh again promises cooperation, and again changes his mind after the insects disappear. Each broken promise reveals something about the ruler: he wants relief from consequences without truly changing his decision.
sections.takeaway: After the gnats and gadflies, it was becoming impossible to pretend this was merely Moses performing tricks.

sections.title: Disease, Boils, and a Storm Like No Other
paragraphs: The fifth plague hits Egypt's livestock with a severe pestilence, while Israel's livestock is protected. Pharaoh even checks the outcome, yet still refuses to act. Then Moses and Aaron toss soot into the air, and painful boils break out on people and animals. Even the Egyptian magic-practicing priests can't stand before Moses because of the boils.

Before the seventh plague, Jehovah gives an important warning: a devastating hailstorm is coming. Egyptian servants who respect the warning hurry their people and animals into shelter. Others leave them outside. The storm strikes with hail and fire, destroys vegetation, and kills those caught in the open. Some later crops are still growing, so the devastation isn't described as every last plant disappearing.

Pharaoh admits that he has sinned and asks Moses to pray for an end to the storm. Moses does. But when the thunder and hail stop, Pharaoh hardens his attitude again. The warnings offered a real opportunity to act wisely, even to Egyptians. Pharaoh's resistance isn't only hurting Israel; it is bringing repeated suffering on his own people.
sections.takeaway: Even in a time of judgment, heeding Jehovah's warning could save lives.

sections.title: Locusts, Darkness, and the Last Warning
paragraphs: By now Pharaoh's officials are pleading with him to let the Israelites go. Egypt is being ruined. Moses announces that locusts will consume what the hail left. A huge swarm covers the land and strips away the remaining greenery. Pharaoh admits wrongdoing and asks for relief. Jehovah removes the locusts, but Pharaoh still will not release all the people to worship.

Then darkness settles over Egypt for three days. It is so intense that people cannot see one another or go about their usual activities. The Israelites, though, have light where they live. Pharaoh offers another compromise: the people may go, but their flocks and herds must remain. Moses refuses to leave behind the animals needed for worship. Pharaoh finally threatens him if he appears again.

Chapter 11 gives the final warning. A tenth plague will strike the firstborn throughout Egypt, from Pharaoh's household to the lowliest family, and even the animals. The Egyptians will urge Israel to leave, and Jehovah gives the Israelites favor in their eyes. After so many refusals, the coming night will change everything.
sections.takeaway: Pharaoh kept bargaining over pieces of Jehovah's command. But the decision was not his to rewrite.

sections.title: Passover Night: The Doorway to Freedom
paragraphs: Before the final plague, Jehovah gives Israel a new annual observance: the Passover. On the tenth day of the month, households choose a sound, one-year-old male sheep or goat. On the fourteenth day they slaughter it, put some of its blood on the two doorposts and upper part of the doorway, roast the meat, and eat it with unleavened bread and bitter greens. They are to eat dressed and ready to leave. These details matter because obedience will protect their families.

That night, Jehovah strikes down the firstborn in Egypt, while the marked Israelite homes are passed over. A great cry rises across the country. Pharaoh summons Moses and Aaron at night and tells the people to go, taking their flocks and herds. The Egyptians urge them out and give them valuable articles and clothing. Families who had lived under brutal oppression now begin to move.

About 600,000 men on foot leave, besides children; a vast mixed company also goes with them. They carry unleavened dough because the departure is so sudden. The account marks the end of a 430-year period of dwelling and sets instructions for observing Passover in future generations. Parents are to explain its meaning to their children. Freedom isn't meant to become a forgotten event: Jehovah wants them to remember how they were delivered.
sections.takeaway: Passover wasn't just a meal before traveling. It became an unforgettable lesson for generations of families.

sections.title: A Cloud by Day, Fire by Night
paragraphs: Israel is finally on the move. Jehovah tells them to set apart every firstborn male for him, a reminder of how he spared Israel's firstborn on Passover night. He also establishes the Festival of Unleavened Bread. Parents are to explain why these observances matter; the memories of deliverance should stay alive as their children grow up.

Jehovah doesn't lead Israel directly along the shorter road through Philistine territory. He knows that warfare could frighten the people into wanting to return to Egypt. Instead, he guides them toward the wilderness and the Red Sea. Moses also carries Joseph's bones, honoring the promise Joseph had asked his descendants to keep so many years earlier.

And how do the people know where to go? Jehovah provides a visible guide: a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night. It never leaves its place before them. The Israelites may not know what lies around the next bend, but they don't have to chart this journey on their own.
sections.takeaway: The shortest route isn't always the wisest one. Jehovah understood what the people could handle.

sections.title: Trapped at the Sea—or So It Seemed
paragraphs: Imagine being newly free and seeing Pharaoh's chariots coming after you. Ahead lies the Red Sea. Behind is Egypt's army. Pharaoh has changed his mind about losing his workforce and sends his forces in pursuit. The Israelites panic, complaining that they were better off staying in Egypt. Moses urges them not to be afraid and to watch how Jehovah will save them.

Jehovah moves the protective pillar and angelic guide between the two camps, keeping the Egyptians from closing in. Moses stretches out his hand, and Jehovah drives the sea back with a strong east wind. The water divides, and the Israelites walk through on dry ground, with walls of water on either side. When the Egyptian forces follow, their chariots become difficult to control.

At Jehovah's direction, Moses stretches out his hand again. The waters return, sweeping away the pursuing Egyptian military forces. Israel reaches the far shore safely. This isn't merely the moment they get away from Pharaoh; it's a moment when the nation sees unmistakable evidence that Jehovah can protect them when no human escape seems possible.
sections.takeaway: They couldn't make a path through the sea. Jehovah opened one.

sections.title: A Victory Song—and Then Bitter Water
paragraphs: Safe on the other side, Moses and the Israelites sing about Jehovah's strength and the defeat of Pharaoh's forces. They speak of Jehovah as a powerful warrior and celebrate that he will lead his redeemed people onward. Miriam, described as a prophetess and Aaron's sister, takes a tambourine and leads the women in a joyful response with tambourines and dancing.

Then the story shifts quickly. After three days in the wilderness, the people cannot find water. At Marah they find water, but it is too bitter to drink. The same people who just celebrated an extraordinary rescue begin complaining. Jehovah shows Moses a piece of wood to throw into the water, and the water becomes drinkable. Jehovah also emphasizes the value of listening to his instructions.

The next stopping place, Elim, has twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees. It's an encouraging contrast to Marah's bitterness. Life after rescue still brings real needs, but the account keeps showing that Jehovah can provide for people while they learn to trust him.
sections.takeaway: A joyful victory didn't mean the wilderness would have no hard days. Jehovah was teaching the people how to rely on him.

sections.title: Bread From Heaven, One Day at a Time
paragraphs: The people become hungry and complain that they would rather have died in Egypt near their cooking pots. Their memories of slavery are being clouded by the discomfort of the journey. Jehovah answers with food: quail appear in the evening, and in the morning a fine, flaky substance covers the ground. The Israelites ask what it is. They call it manna.

Each household gathers what it needs for that day. Extra manna kept overnight on ordinary days spoils, teaching them not to hoard it. But on the sixth day they collect a double portion, and it keeps for the seventh day, the Sabbath, when none will fall. Some people still go looking on the seventh day and find nothing. Jehovah is teaching them to trust both his provision and his schedule.

The manna tastes like wafers made with honey. Israel will eat it for forty years, until they reach inhabited land. Jehovah also instructs that a sample be kept as a reminder for future generations. Food becomes a daily lesson: today's needs matter, and so does learning not to live in constant fear about tomorrow.
sections.takeaway: Jehovah wasn't only feeding Israel. He was teaching an entire nation to trust his daily care.

sections.title: Water From Rock and Help in Battle
paragraphs: At Rephidim the people have no water, and once again they quarrel with Moses. They ask why he led them out of Egypt if they and their children might die of thirst. Moses appeals to Jehovah. Jehovah tells him to take his rod and strike a rock at Horeb. Water comes out for the people. The place receives names recalling their quarreling and their testing of Jehovah.

Then an enemy appears: the Amalekites attack Israel. Joshua leads the fighting men while Moses stands on a hill holding up the rod of the true God. As long as Moses keeps his hands raised, Israel prevails. When he grows tired, Aaron and Hur help support his hands until sunset, and Joshua defeats the attackers.

Moses builds an altar and names it Jehovah-nissi, meaning 'Jehovah Is My Signal Pole.' The chapter contains two very different emergencies—thirst and battle—but they share the same lesson. Israel cannot survive the wilderness by human strength alone, and even Moses benefits from people willing to support him.
sections.takeaway: Jehovah provided water—and Aaron and Hur showed the value of holding up someone who was tired.

sections.title: Jethro's Advice: Share the Load
paragraphs: Moses' father-in-law Jethro hears what Jehovah has done for Israel and comes to the camp. He brings Zipporah and Moses' two sons, Gershom and Eliezer. Moses tells him about the trouble and the rescue from Egypt. Jethro rejoices and praises Jehovah, and they share a meal together in the presence of God.

The next day Jethro sees Moses spending the whole day settling the people's disputes. There is a line of cases and just one exhausted judge. Jethro points out that this arrangement isn't good for Moses or the people. He advises Moses to teach Jehovah's standards and appoint capable, trustworthy men who hate dishonest gain to handle ordinary cases.

Moses listens. Judges are appointed over groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens; especially difficult matters can still come to Moses. The nation is growing, and its organization needs to grow too. It's a lovely example of humility in leadership: Moses doesn't have to do every job himself to be faithful.
sections.takeaway: Good leadership includes listening to wise advice and trusting capable people with responsibility.
